The delivery of data for analyses in high-energy physics often relies on a centralized data management system, which can be challenging to scale to meet the needs of large collaborations.  To address this issue, a new service called ServiceX was developed to provide on-demand data delivery.  By utilizing a distributed network of data caches, ServiceX ensures that analyses can access required data, even if it's not locally available, by transferring it from other locations in the network.  This approach enables analyses to run independently of the system administrators, allowing them to choose the data delivery method that best suits their needs.  To date, ServiceX has been successfully deployed in the ATLAS collaboration and has processed over 1.5 petabytes of data, supporting more than 1,000 analyses.  This paper will provide an overview of ServiceX's design, functionality, and performance results.  It will also discuss the benefits and lessons learned from its deployment in the ATLAS collaboration and its potential for use in other experiments.  Furthermore, the service's potential for broader application in the data-intensive science community will be explored. differentiate through its actor's policy allows for the direct optimization of
the mean reward. Our analysis demonstrates that DART converges at a rate of

outperforms existing $\mathcal{O}(K^{-1})$ algorithms in mean reward
optimization. Furthermore, DART's differentiable architecture enables the
derivation of uncertainty estimates for policy decisions, enabling the
application of Bayesian decision-making principles. We validate DART's efficacy
by comparing it to state-of-the-art algorithms in both mean and total reward
optimization on a range of benchmark tasks. Additionally, we showcase the
utility of DART's uncertainty estimates in a Bayesian decision-making

Learning from an expert's partial guidance via demonstrations is a common approach in imitation learning, yet it often falls short in replicating the expert's behavior when the underlying state and action spaces are extensive. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework called SoftDICE, which utilizes a generative model to create a soft version of the expert's policy, thereby allowing for more efficient learning. By incorporating a generative model, SoftDICE can effectively recover an expert's policy using limited demonstrations, even in scenarios with vast state and action spaces. Additionally, SoftDICE can be trained in a semi-supervised manner, leveraging a large set of generated data to enhance the learning process. We demonstrate the efficacy of SoftDICE through its successful application in multiple continuous control tasks, outperforming existing imitation learning methods. Notably, SoftDICE can achieve superior results with as few as ten expert demonstrations, and its semi-supervised training approach can further reduce the required demonstrations to a mere one. We believe that URLB will drive innovation in unsupervised RL research, leading to the development of more effective algorithms that can efficiently learn and generalize in complex environments. To address this challenge, we developed a novel deep learning approach that leverages the strengths of both convolutional neural networks and clustering techniques to identify bird species from images. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we applied it to the iBird 2020 Bird Species Classification Challenge and achieved a top-3 ranking, with a test accuracy of 92.88% and a top-3 error rate of 7.12%.  Our results demonstrate the potential of deep learning-based clustering techniques for identifying bird species from images.  Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to other computer vision tasks involving image classification, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with minimal modifications.  To facilitate reproducible research, we have made our source code available on GitHub. The collapse of modes in generative models is a long-standing issue that has been extensively studied, yet a widely accepted definition remains elusive. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to characterizing mode collapse based on the Hessian eigenvalues of the generator's output. This method is highly effective in identifying mode collapse and can be seamlessly integrated into existing training processes. Our analysis reveals that mode collapse is closely linked to the Hessian's largest eigenvalues, which are indicative of the generator's instability in specific regions of the input space. To mitigate this instability, we propose a simple yet efficient solution involving a low-cost Hessian regularization technique. This regularization method can be easily incorporated into various generative models, including GANs and VAEs, and is computationally efficient, requiring only a single additional backward pass during training. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in preventing mode collapse and improving the quality of generated images. In graph representation learning, a crucial task is to embed nodes into a continuous space where similarities between connected nodes are reflected. A common approach to achieving this is to utilize random walks, which have been used in various methods such as DeepWalk and node2vec. However, a significant limitation of these methods is that they do not account for variations in graph density. This oversight can lead to suboptimal results, as embeddings from denser graphs may not generalize well to other graphs with different densities. To address this issue, we propose a new method called DensWalk, which incorporates graph density into the random walk process. By doing so, DensWalk can effectively learn node representations that can be applied to graphs with varying densities. The proposed method is evaluated on multiple real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. We introduce Domain Prompt Learning (DPL), a straightforward yet effective approach
to adapt pre-trained models for zero-shot classification across various domains.
DPL leverages a few labeled images within each domain to fine-tune the model's
prompt, thereby enhancing its domain adaptability. By combining DPL with the
pre-trained CLIP model, we create a high-performance, zero-shot image
classifier, dubbed DPL-CLIP, which surpasses the performance of its predecessor
in image classification tasks. Notably, DPL-CLIP achieves state-of-the-art results
on the Domain Robustness Benchmark, outperforming the current benchmark by a
substantial margin of 5.2% on average. Furthermore, DPL-CLIP exhibits exceptional
generalizability across various domains, as evidenced by its superior performance
on the Domain Robustness Benchmark, particularly in scenarios involving
adversarial perturbations, data augmentation, and domain shifts. The code and
pre-trained models for DPL-CLIP are publicly available on the GitHub repository.

The acquisition process of scanning-mode image modalities can be significantly accelerated by employing interlacing methods, which involve capturing and processing image data in non-contiguous segments. However, this approach necessitates the development of specialized algorithms to reconstruct these segments into a unified image. In this research, we introduce a novel deep learning framework that seamlessly integrates the reconstruction and denoising of interlaced data. Our method leverages a dual-branch architecture, which simultaneously decomposes the noisy image into a clean version and a residual error. The residual error is then used to reconstruct the image, while the clean version serves as the initial image. Our framework is trained end-to-end, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world interlaced data. Furthermore, we conduct a comparative analysis with existing denoising techniques and demonstrate that our method not only enhances image quality but also reduces acquisition time. The transcriptional process is a complex, multi-step phenomenon that involves the coordinated actions of numerous proteins. While ChIP-Seq data can provide insight into the spatiotemporal distribution of these proteins, this information is typically insufficient to fully explain the underlying transcriptional mechanisms. To address this limitation, we developed a novel approach that integrates ChIP-Seq data with information about transcription speed and temporal protein activity to reconstruct the temporal profiles of key transcriptional proteins. Our method, which utilizes a combination of Gaussian process regression and Bayesian inference, can be applied to both individual and paired ChIP-Seq datasets. When tested on a dataset featuring the transcription factor TFIIS, our approach successfully recreated the temporal profiles of TFIIS and other associated proteins, including Pol-II, TFIID, and TFIIB. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our method can be applied to paired datasets to infer the temporal profiles of proteins involved in alternative splicing. Overall, our approach provides a powerful tool for elucidating the underlying mechanisms of transcriptional regulation. We introduce the DDF inspector-executor framework, a high-performance approach for sparse matrix multiplication and solving linear systems. By leveraging distributed-memory environments, DDF inspector-executor efficiently handles sparse matrix operations. Unlike traditional methods that require explicit matrix multiplication and triangular system resolution, our framework enables the execution of these operations concurrently. DDF inspector-executor effectively optimizes sparse matrix performance by minimizing communication overhead and maximizing computation efficiency. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through the successful execution of a Krylov subspace-based conjugate gradient solver on a large-scale sparse linear system. The performance of DDF inspector-executor is evaluated on the NERSC's Cori supercomputer, showcasing its ability to efficiently solve complex sparse linear systems with millions of non-zero elements. This study explores the application of federated learning in edge computing for training machine learning models using data from connected vehicles. We investigate the impact of various data collection strategies on model accuracy and training efficiency, specifically comparing centralized and decentralized approaches. Our analysis reveals that incorporating connected vehicles through edge federated learning can effectively reduce the aggregation of model parameters, with improvements ranging from 20% to 50% when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a smaller number of vehicles can still achieve comparable results by sharing parameters in a decentralized manner. Our findings also indicate that a more efficient data collection approach, which involves less data and lower communication, can still yield superior model performance. We validate these results through extensive simulations using real-world data from the CitySeg dataset. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential of federated learning in facilitating collaborative model training among connected vehicles while addressing data privacy and communication constraints. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the development of intelligent transportation systems that can better serve the needs of modern transportation. sampling, our approach ensures the privatized data is deterministic and free of

algorithms using both our privatized data and the original dataset. The results
show that our method can produce accurate and reliable outcomes, with some
machine learning models even outperforming those trained on the original data.

datasets, allowing researchers to work with anonymized data without the risks
associated with using real-world data. The accompanying code for our research is

Recent advancements in transformer-based models have led to outstanding performance in numerous NLP tasks, but their high computational requirements have hindered their application in real-time environments. To address this limitation, we introduce DAE-Former, a novel transformer architecture that leverages domain adaptation to enhance efficiency. DAE-Former incorporates a domain adaptation encoder that captures semantic information from a target domain, represented as a set of discrete tokens, and a self-attention module that utilizes these tokens to generate efficient attention weights. By decoupling domain knowledge from model parameters, DAE-Former achieves improved performance while reducing computational costs. Experimental results demonstrate DAE-Former's superiority over traditional self-attention methods, and its ability to match state-of-the-art domain adaptation models while operating at a lower computational complexity. Deep neural networks have been successfully applied to numerous tasks, but they often require substantial amounts of labeled data for training, a major obstacle in many real-world applications. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Deep aPCE, a two-stage method that leverages Approximate Probabilistic Collocation to create a surrogate model. This model is then refined using a limited number of labeled data points. By combining the strengths of deep neural networks and approximate collocation, Deep aPCE offers improved accuracy compared to traditional methods, all while requiring less labeled data for training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments on regression tasks, showcasing its ability to produce highly accurate predictions with significantly less labeled data required. Additionally, Deep aPCE enables the incorporation of probabilistic uncertainty, allowing for more reliable predictions and enabling applications that require confidence measures. To facilitate the use of our method, we provide a publicly available implementation. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/Deep-aPCE/Deep-aPCE. Artificial neural networks' vulnerability to noise has been extensively studied, 
with most research focusing on the impact of white noise. This paper delves into 
the effects of non-white, correlated noise types on the performance of artificial 
neural networks, specifically those designed for classification tasks. We examine 
the influence of noise with Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions on the 
network's accuracy, using a support vector machine as a reference point. To assess 
the impact of noise, we employ a modified version of the MNIST dataset with added 
noise during training. Our findings demonstrate that the performance of artificial 
neural networks varies significantly depending on the type of noise and the network 
architecture used. This research aims to contribute to the development of more 
robust artificial neural networks capable of functioning effectively in noisy 
environments. The code used in this study is publicly available on the GitHub 
platform. We also provide a comprehensive guide for readers to replicate our 
results. This paper's conclusions are supported by the presented experimental data. 
Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering the impact of noise 
on the performance of artificial neural networks in real-world applications.

Machine Learning, Deep Learning.

This approach is typically used in the context of model-free learning, where experiences are replayed in isolation. Our research explores an alternative method, drawing inspiration from the "state-based replay" technique, which involves storing and reusing specific states to inform decision-making. We demonstrate that a small set of strategically selected states can provide a significant advantage in minimizing prediction errors, even in complex continuous control tasks. Furthermore, we show that these states can be learned efficiently through a process of exploration, resulting in a highly effective and sample-efficient approach to learning. Our findings are supported by experiments conducted in both simulated and real-world environments, with notable results achieved in the context of robotic manipulation. The code used in our research is publicly available on the GitHub repository, https://github.com/asharakeh-research/state-based-replay. Our research has the potential to open up new avenues for research in the field of reinforcement learning, particularly in the context of continuous control. The implications of our findings extend beyond the specific problem of robotic manipulation, with potential applications in a wide range of continuous control tasks. The key to our approach lies in the strategic selection of states to inform decision-making, rather than relying on arbitrary past experiences. By incorporating this module into the PointNet++ framework, we demonstrate its effectiveness in improving 3D object detection accuracy. Specifically, we present a dual-branch attention module, which integrates spatial and channel-wise attention mechanisms into the network's branch convolutional layers. The proposed attention module can be seamlessly integrated into the PointNet++ framework, yielding improved performance in 3D object detection. Experimental results on the KITTI dataset confirm the efficacy of the proposed attention module, achieving a 2.5% and 1.5% increase in mAP for car and pedestrian classes, respectively, when compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Human visual attention patterns are crucial for understanding how people interact with visual content, particularly in professional settings like image inspection. In many fields, such as quality control, experts are often under pressure to quickly review images within a limited timeframe. To understand how these time constraints impact visual attention, we conducted a study with 30 participants who had to identify defects in images of printed circuit boards under different time pressures. Our analysis revealed that time constraints significantly affect the visual attention patterns and defect detection accuracy of the inspectors. Specifically, shorter time limits led to more focused attention but also reduced overall accuracy, while longer time limits enabled a more thorough inspection but increased mental workload. These findings suggest that time pressure can be optimized by striking a balance between efficiency and thoroughness. The implications of these results for image inspection tasks and defect detection in general are substantial, particularly in scenarios where time is of the essence. The insights gained from this study can inform the design of more effective image inspection systems and improve defect detection accuracy. Deep learning applications are becoming increasingly prevalent in edge devices, 
such as smartphones and smart sensors, due to their ability to process data in real-time. 
However, the limited storage capacity and computational capabilities of these devices pose significant challenges for deep learning models. 
To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach that combines knowledge distillation and model pruning to optimize the performance of edge devices. 
Our method involves distilling the knowledge of a large teacher model into a smaller student model, 
and then utilizing the student's weights as a soft constraint to guide the model pruning process. 
This approach enables the student model to achieve higher compression ratios and improved accuracy compared to traditional pruning methods. 
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on various deep learning models, 
including ResNet-18, ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-B0, using the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. 
The results show that our method achieves higher compression ratios and comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art methods. 
Furthermore, the proposed approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, 
making it a versatile and efficient solution for deep learning applications in edge devices.

The results show that our model achieves a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to existing benchmarks. It inherits Lenia's ability to incorporate parameter changes within its own dynamics, allowing for emergent behavior and self-modification. As cells evolve, they can shift between different states, and the flow-based approach enables the propagation of information across multiple dimensions. This synergy gives rise to a diverse range of patterns, including intricate structures and adaptive processes. Furthermore, we explore the potential of Flow Lenia as a model for neural networks, where neurons can transform into different states and adapt to their surroundings. Our research also touches on the broader implications of this framework in the context of artificial life and its potential applications in the future. User-item interactions are often influenced by the context in which they occur, a factor that existing recommendation methods frequently overlook. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach called BC Loss, a technique that utilizes context-aware contrastive learning to enhance the representation of users and items within recommendation systems. By drawing inspiration from the Context-Aware Language Model, we develop a method to incorporate contextual information into the embedding space, where items are grouped according to their context. Within these groups, items are positioned closer together when shared in the same context, and farther apart when not. To achieve this, we employ a contrastive learning objective that encourages close proximity between contextualized items and pushes apart non-contextualized items. Furthermore, we incorporate a temporal context-aware objective to capture the temporal dynamics of user interactions, a feature that is particularly beneficial for sequential recommendation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of BC Loss in surpassing state-of-the-art performance across a range of benchmark datasets. The accompanying source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-KEG/BC_LOSS. Theoretical analysis reveals that the algorithm achieves a sublinear convergence rate, and numerical experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing policies for both discrete and continuous action spaces. Furthermore, PMD-PD outperforms existing methods in solving a range of constrained Markov decision processes, including those with high-dimensional action spaces. The algorithm's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yszhangcb/pmpd. Additionally, a Python implementation of the algorithm can be accessed via the PyMPCD library. This study introduces a novel optical flow estimation technique, referred to as SMURF, which leverages a deep learning approach to address the issue of motion occurring outside the frame. By utilizing a convolutional neural network, SMURF is capable of processing both local and global image information to achieve accurate motion estimates. The proposed method employs a two-stage training strategy, initially learning to estimate optical flow within a fixed frame of reference and subsequently refining this ability to handle out-of-frame motion. The results indicate that SMURF surpasses the performance of conventional optical flow estimation methods, while also outshining a prominent neural network-based approach. The proposed technique exhibits exceptional robustness in handling motion outside the frame, demonstrating a notable improvement of 10-20% in accuracy compared to the next best method. The source code and trained models for SMURF are made available for public access on the GitHub platform. The project can be accessed at: https://github.com/DeepMotionLab/SMURF. We introduce a novel approach to detecting symptoms in dialog systems by
leveraging knowledge graphs. Our method involves training a model to identify
symptoms based on contextual dialog information and knowledge graph embeddings.
The model combines knowledge graph and dialog embeddings to predict symptoms.
To validate our approach, we developed a new benchmark dataset for symptom
detection in dialog systems, which includes a knowledge graph and dialog corpus.
Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating the knowledge graph significantly
enhances symptom detection accuracy. Moreover, our model outperforms baseline
models that rely solely on dialog information. The results of our study indicate
that knowledge graph information can improve symptom detection in dialog systems. 
Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/DeepSaffron/KGSD.

Capturing images in rapidly changing dynamic scenes often results in blurry images due to motion between the subject and camera. Advanced image restoration techniques can improve the clarity of these images, but they can also introduce artifacts that alter the image's color and texture. By applying this prediction to images with high restoration potential, we can restore them first and then combine the restored image with the original blurry image using a weighted average. This approach enables the preservation of sharp details in static areas while enhancing the overall image quality. Our experiments demonstrate that this technique outperforms existing methods in restoring images from dynamic scenes, as evident in our results on real-world images and the SIDD dataset. The Visual Question Answering task seeks to develop intelligent systems that can comprehend and respond to human-like queries based on visual information. Despite significant advancements in this field, existing VQA models still face a major limitation: they are unable to generalize effectively to novel scenarios, hindering their practical application. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the power of meta-learning to enhance VQA model performance on unseen tasks. By framing VQA as a meta-learning problem, we can create a more adaptable model capable of handling diverse question types and generalizing to unencountered data. Our proposed method, which incorporates a meta-training and meta-testing framework, utilizes a dynamic attention mechanism to identify key image regions and selects relevant question words for accurate answer prediction. Comprehensive experiments on the VQA v2 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which achieves a notable 3.5% improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our model exhibits superior generalizability to unseen questions, outperforming existing solutions by a substantial 6.5% in the zero-shot setting. We introduce Temporal Shift Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a novel approach to temporal learning that diverges from traditional methods. Unlike these methods, TSRL does not necessitate the use of additional parameters to learn temporal relationships, such as the incorporation of temporal convolutional layers or recurrent neural networks. Instead, it leverages the inherent temporal structure of the environment's state and rewards to guide policy decision-making. TSRL can be seamlessly integrated into existing reinforcement learning frameworks, and we demonstrate its efficacy by incorporating it into a prominent model-free algorithm, Soft Actor-Critic, to tackle the challenging control tasks in the MuJoCo physics simulator. TSRL enables SAC to achieve superior performance, surpassing state-of-the-art results in these tasks, and we provide an in-depth analysis of TSRL's theoretical underpinnings. Furthermore, we showcase TSRL's versatility by applying it to a range of reinforcement learning problems, including both continuous and discrete action spaces, and we highlight its potential to be adapted for other model-free and model-based reinforcement learning methods. This study examines the effectiveness of knowledge distillation from an optimization standpoint, focusing on the convergence of student and teacher models. We investigate the learning process of student models trained on data generated by student, teacher, and intermediate models. We find that teacher models with intermediate convergence serve as better instructors than fully converged models or student models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating ensembles of student models can achieve convergence without requiring a fully converged teacher model. Additionally, we propose a novel distillation method, 'warm-up distillation,' which leverages an ensemble of student models as an intermediate teacher. We validate our findings through experiments on various models, including ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and EfficientNet-B0, and observe consistent improvements in student model performance. Notably, our approach yields a 0.7% improvement in ResNet-18's accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset, with only 0.1% increase in training time compared to traditional knowledge distillation methods. This paper introduces a novel attention-based framework for hyperspectral image denoising, which leverages the spectral-spatial attention block (SSAB) to enhance denoising performance. The former module adapts the standard convolutional layer to adaptively focus on both spatial and spectral features, while the latter enables cross-channel interaction, allowing the network to capture complex relationships between spectral bands. The SSAB block is then integrated into a U-Net architecture, and our proposed SSAB-Net is trained using a denoising loss function. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SSAB-Net in removing Gaussian noise from hyperspectral images, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual quality and quantitative metrics. sequence of actions. We demonstrate that our framework can be applied to a broad 
category of games with global regularity, encompassing potential, weighted potential,

the context of zero-sum games. Furthermore, we show that the regret of Q-learning

cooperative games. Specifically, we establish convergence in potential games, 
deriving a novel result for the Gomory-Hu tree in weighted potential games. Our

Nash equilibrium of Q-learning in dynamic games. The key innovation in our work 
is the development of a framework that enables the analysis of last-iterate 
convergence in a wide range of games with a broad class of regularity conditions.

In this research, we introduce a novel FMM-based method for identifying disease-associated genes by leveraging a wide range of genomic data. The proposed framework utilizes a probabilistic model to assign genes to distinct clusters based on their correlation with disease phenotypes across multiple studies. The clustering process is grounded in the multivariate normal distribution, allowing for the derivation of the log-likelihood function and its gradient. The resulting optimization problem is solved using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, which we demonstrate through a simulation study and a practical application to identify genes associated with breast cancer. The findings indicate that our proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of clustering accuracy and gene ranking. These insights have important implications for PINN users and developers, enabling more informed selection of model parameters and potentially leading to improved performance. The study also highlights the need for further research into PINN's scalability limitations and potential workarounds. Digital libraries have become increasingly popular, but their search and recommendation systems often struggle to meet users' needs. By examining click behavior on digital library landing pages, we can gain valuable insights to enhance these systems. This study investigates the click patterns of users in the National Digital Library of China, focusing on the differences between users who click documents and those who engage with other interactive elements. We discovered that users who click documents are more likely to interact with search results, whereas those who explore interactive features are more interested in the library's offerings. Our findings suggest that digital libraries can improve their search and recommendation capabilities by incorporating user behavior analysis and incorporating features that showcase the library's content. These recommendations are supported by real-world experiments conducted on the NDLC platform. The study's conclusions and practical applications have the potential to contribute to the development of more effective digital libraries. This study delves into generating Bird's Eye View maps from single-image inputs,
utilizing both vision transformers and Convolutional Neural Networks for comparison.
Our investigation centers around the BEV map generation process, specifically how
different architectures produce these maps, and whether they share common
characteristics. To this end, we analyze the attention patterns of vision
transformers and compare them to the output of CNNs, and find that the BEV maps
generated by these models are not only distinct, but also lack a unified
characteristic. To address this disparity, we propose a novel approach to
integrating CNN and transformer-based features, which we term the
Multi-Modal Transformer (MMT) architecture. Our results demonstrate that the
MMT outperforms both the CNN and transformer-based models in terms of accuracy,
and showcases its ability to adapt to various tasks, including object detection and
BEV segmentation. Furthermore, we find that the MMT can effectively leverage the
strengths of both the CNN and transformer-based models, and that the attention
patterns of the MMT are more interpretable than those of the transformer-based
models. Our code and models are publicly available on GitHub. The source code can
be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyuinstitute/MultiModalTransformer. The
pre-trained models can be downloaded from the Google Colab environment. The
corresponding author can be contacted via email at [zhangyin@cs.cmu.edu](mailto:zhangyin@cs.cmu.edu).

The task of novel class detection in image classification involves identifying images from unseen classes without the benefit of labeled training data from those classes. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called OPG, which generates pseudo-unseen samples by adapting a pre-trained classifier to produce images that are misclassified as belonging to unknown classes. By leveraging these generated pseudo samples, OPG trains a binary classifier to distinguish between seen and unseen classes. To further enhance detection accuracy, OPG also incorporates a self-supervised learning mechanism that utilizes the seen classes to improve the quality of the pseudo samples. Comprehensive experiments on established benchmarks demonstrate that OPG outperforms existing methods, with the greatest improvements observed in scenarios with limited seen classes. We introduce a novel cost constructor that leverages the depth information from a pre-trained depth estimator to enhance the cost calculation in optical flow estimation tasks.
